title: MiniMax Uses Its Internal Model to Take On Cryptography: Turning Paper Attacks into Second-Level Real-World Exploits; NIST Competition Algorithm Cracked for Real for the First Time

content_html:
MiniMax's research team had its latest internal model do something that previously almost only top cryptographers would dare to imagine: launch systematic automated cryptanalysis against frontier cryptographic schemes. The results were unexpectedly hardcore: the model discovered a set of previously undisclosed weaknesses in algorithmic constructions and pushed some attack methods that had remained only at the theoretical, paper-only stage all the way to a state where they could be actually executed in seconds or minutes. In other words, attacks that once required huge amounts of manpower and time and might not even work were now run through by AI on the spot.

The results unfolded along three main lines. The first was the most eye-catching: the model for the first time actually broke multiple candidate algorithms from past NIST international cryptographic standardization competitions—designs that had previously had no known practical attacks, meaning defenses specially selected for international standards were, for the first time, found by AI to have cracks. The second targeted the academic frontier: for schemes published in recent top international cryptography conferences and journals and for competition-winning designs, the model achieved efficient ciphertext forgery or key recovery, and set a new record for the highest number of broken rounds of novel block ciphers. The third returned to the oldest frontal battlefield: by mining hidden algebraic structures and layering on system-level engineering optimizations to solve the classic hard mathematical problems on which public-key cryptography rests, it for the first time cracked dozens of high-level instances of international public challenges that previously had no public solutions, with measured speeds hundreds to tens of thousands of times faster than current state-of-the-art solvers.

What is worth noting is the sense of boundaries in this research. MiniMax emphasized that the analysis was aimed only at frontier academic schemes, historical competition candidate designs, and public-parameter challenges, and did not touch any systems actually in use; the relevant results have been shared with the scheme authors, and after the reasoning traces are organized and verified, they will be made public in the form of a technical report and code. The deepest implication of this may be that even cryptography, a field regarded as a bastion of human intellect, is beginning to be treated by AI as an exam problem that can be automatically conquered—mathematical constructions that their designers believed to be secure are being re-examined one by one by a tireless model.
